beats.say: Why does a business need a moat? Because rivals keep attacking any business that earns a lot for the money put in. Warren Buffett wrote that in his two thousand and seven letter. He is one of the most famous investors in the world. For many years, he ran a big group of companies in America.
beats.cap: Why does a business need a moat? Because rivals keep attacking any business that earns a lot for the money put in. Warren Buffett wrote that in his 2007 letter. He is one of the most famous investors in the world. For many years, he ran a big group of companies in America (Berkshire Hathaway).

beats.say: What is a moat made of? Buffett gave two examples: very low costs, or a famous brand known all over the world.

beats.say: In his nineteen eighty six letter, Buffett wrote about GEICO, an American car insurer. Our rupee picture, for nineteen eighty six: customers paid GEICO for car insurance. For every hundred rupees, only twenty three rupees and fifty paise went on running costs. Many big rivals spent about fifteen rupees more. Why does that gap matter?
beats.cap: In his 1986 letter, Buffett wrote about GEICO, an American car insurer. Our rupee picture, for 1986: customers paid GEICO for car insurance. For every ₹100, only ₹23.50 went on running costs. Many big rivals spent about ₹15 more (about ₹38.50, our arithmetic). Why does that gap matter?

Why does that gap matter?

beats.say: Our reading: with costs that low, GEICO could charge less, or keep more. Buffett called that gap a kind of moat. Did any rival ever cross it?

beats.say: Buffett first learned about GEICO in nineteen fifty one. Its low costs amazed him. In his twenty thirteen letter, he wrote that those low costs were still there. That is more than sixty years, by our arithmetic. Rivals, he wrote, were unable to cross this moat. So what is the second kind of water?

beats.say: A famous brand. In his nineteen ninety three letter, Buffett pointed to Coca Cola and Gillette. Out of every hundred soft drinks in the world, about forty four were Coke. Of all the money spent on razor blades, Gillette got more than sixty in every hundred. Why does a famous name keep rivals out?

beats.say: Yes. In India, people keep their shares, small pieces of companies, in online lockers. Every one sits with just two companies: C D S L or N S D L. A newcomer needs a licence that is not being handed out, our August twenty twenty six article says. But the same article shows the regulator can cut some of C D S L's fees. So can a strong moat be fake?

beats.say: How do you spot a fake moat? Watch what happens when rivals really try. Buffett wrote that business history is full of Roman candles: companies whose moats only looked real, and were soon crossed. A Roman candle is a firework: bright for a moment, then dark.

beats.say: Does a moat last forever? No. Every day, it gets a little deeper, or a little shallower. Buffett's two thousand and five letter says each of his businesses grows weaker or stronger daily. One day's change is too small to see. Added up, it is enormous.

beats.say: How do you test any business? Ask our three questions. One: can a rival with money and time copy what protects it? Two: does it have to be rebuilt again and again? Three: does it walk out of the door with one person? A strong moat answers no, no and no.

beats.say: Quick recap. What is a moat? What keeps rivals out. Why does a business need one? Rivals attack whoever earns well. What is it made of? Low costs, a brand, a lock, a crowd, a licence. A fake moat? Soon crossed. One star? Not a moat. Forever? No. The test? Copy, rebuild, one person.
